chapter_theme: Shame over wrongdoing is the distinguishing mark of a human being and the seat of worth. It ranks above life, conduct and the whole earth, and those without it only imitate being alive.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar: its definition (1011), its excellence (1012-1014), the eminence of those who have it (1015), their deeds (1016-1017), and the lowness of those without it (1018-1020).

1011.reading: Shame is being ashamed through one's actions; anything other is the shame of women of the bright brow.
1011.nuance: The verse separates moral shame from bodily modesty and assigns the second to women. Whichever women are meant, the distinction is gendered.

positions.position: The women are honoured family women, and he rejects explicitly the reading that they are courtesans.
They are courtesans, good only in their brow, so that any other shame is merely like theirs.
positions.quote: அழகிய நுதலினாலே நல்லாராகிய கணிகையர் நாணத்தோ டொக்கும்.

1012.reading: Food, clothing and the rest are no different for any living being, and the distinction of humans is having shame.
1012.nuance: The verse seems to separate humans from other life, but the commentators draw the line within humanity. Parimelazhagar contrasts all people with good people, and Manakkudavar contrasts base people with leaders. Parimelazhagar lists the rest of what is shared as sleep, fear and desire.

1013.reading: As all lives are fixed on flesh, worth is fixed on the good called shame.

positions.position: ஊன் is the body: worth can't have effect without shame, as a soul can't without a body. He reports ஊண் as a variant.
positions.quote: உயிர் உடம்பொடு கூடியல்லது பயனெய்தாத வாறுபோலச் சால்பு நாணோடு கூடியல்லது பயன் எய்தாது

positions.position: The word is food: living things want food above all, and worth wants shame above all.
positions.quote: பலவகை உயிரும் மேற்கூறிய எல்லாவற்றினும் உண்டியைக் கருதிற்று

1014.reading: Isn't shame an ornament to the worthy? Without it, isn't a proud walk a disease?
1014.nuance: அணி and பிணி rhyme. Parimelazhagar makes this a disease for those who have to watch it. A walk, in other words, is public property and judged by the watcher.

1015.reading: The world calls those who feel shame for others' disgrace as for their own the dwelling of shame.
1015.nuance: This enlarges shame beyond guilt: one feels it for what one did not do. Moral concern here can't be reduced to self-regard.

1016.reading: The high don't care for the wide world unless they have shame for a fence.
1016.nuance: The verse can mean they would take shame rather than the world, or that they won't want the world without it; Parimelazhagar holds the first and reports the second. Pope's couplet follows the second. Kalaignar has shame as the best of protections, with no choice involved.

1017.reading: Those ruled by shame will give up life for shame, and won't give up shame for life.
1017.nuance: The syntax folds on itself like the choice it describes. நாணாள்பவர் can be 'those who wield shame', as a commander does, and not those who are ruled by it. Kalaignar glosses the object as மானம், showing how closely the two virtues run.

1018.reading: If one is not ashamed of what makes others ashamed, it's a fault that virtue itself would be ashamed of.
1018.nuance: நாண recurs and virtue becomes a person who blushes. Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar read this as virtue leaving such a man, since virtue doesn't approach the shameless, so shame is a precondition of virtue and not one of its parts.

1019.reading: A lapse in principle burns one's lineage, and lasting shamelessness burns every good thing.
1019.nuance: Parimelazhagar draws the ranking out: destroying shame is worse than destroying conduct, which is significant given the rank chapter 14 gives conduct. Fire (சுடும்) is used for both.

1020.reading: The movements of those with no shame within are like a wooden puppet feigning life by its string.
1020.nuance: The pun is on நாண், which means both shame and string. The puppet has the one thing the man lacks, as Parimelazhagar notes, in a neat inversion. It leaves a man without shame to be moved from outside.

links.note: 1017 says the shame-bearing would give up life before shame. 1251 says that love's axe breaks the door barred by shame. The same supreme barrier falls in the book of love, and the whole book of love depends on that collapse.

A nearly identical ranking is made for two virtues. 969 gives up life for மானம் and 1017 for நாண். Kalaignar's gloss of 1017 even uses மானம். The verses suggest honour and shame are the outward and inward faces of a single conviction.
Shame is ornament in both. 1014 calls it the ornament of the worthy, and 1089 asks what other ornaments a woman with shame could need. The same figure crosses gender and books.

315 asks what good knowledge is if one doesn't treat another's pain as one's own. 1015 makes the same move for disgrace: treating another's blame as one's own. Both make moral identification the test of the higher quality.
Both first state what is common to all life, and then find சிறப்பு. For 972 that is deeds, and for 1012 it is shame. Read together, the Kural's account of human distinction becomes specific.
The soul's hold on the body is the simile for virtue's bond in both: in 73 love's tie is like that of life to bone, and in 1013 worth holds on to shame in the same way.

Wood is used twice for those without inner quality. The courtesy chapter's man is a tree in 997, and the shameless man here a wooden puppet. The puppet is worse, since it has been shaped to look alive.

Personified moral forces flee from the faulty. In 924, Shame the good woman turns her back on the drunk, and in 1018 Virtue herself blushes and departs from one who doesn't blush. Shame is first the one who flees and then the condition for virtue's staying.

source_issues: 1015: no Manakkudavar commentary is aligned to this verse.
1016: the Manakkudavar text is marked [#] and nearly identical to Parimelazhagar's gloss.
1017: Kalaignar's text ends with a stray 1018.
1011: Pope's gloss has 'bashfulness of virtuous maids', from Parimelazhagar, a reading that Manakkudavar contradicts.
